valuation.net_debt_note: EV = market cap + latest borrowings. Screener's public page does not split cash out of other assets, so cash is not netted off; investments are shown separately.

dcf.method: 5-year FCFF: EBITDA - tax on EBIT - capex - change in net working capital; growth fades linearly from the starting rate to the year-5 rate; Gordon terminal value; equity = EV - borrowings.

inputs.growth_basis: median of 3-year, 5-year and TTM sales growth, capped 0-30%
inputs.capex_rule: depreciation + new sales / fixed-asset turnover (median of the last three years)

reverse_dcf.note: Constant sales growth for five years, at the base margin and the same WACC and terminal growth, that makes the DCF equal today's EV.

blocks.text: [F] CFF Fluid Control Ltd (formerly Flash Forge Fluid Control Pvt Ltd, incorporated February 2012) manufactures and services shipboard machinery, critical component systems and test facilities for submarines and surface ships for the defence sector (RATING). [F] Its product scope covers fluid and platform control, sonar, weapons handling, submarine communications, steering, HVAC and other mechanical and electro-mechanical equipment, with support from factory acceptance and trials through refit (RATING) (SCREENER).

[F] It makes money in two ways: supply of equipment for new-build ships and submarines under tenders, and spares, maintenance, upgrades and refit support over the long life of naval platforms (RATING). [F] CRISIL describes the business as depending 'entirely on tenders from customers' (RATING). [AI] In economic terms it is a tender-driven, build-to-order engineering subcontractor to Indian naval shipbuilding and dockyards, with a lifecycle-support tail. It is not a platform prime contractor.

items: End-market split: [F] effectively 100% defence/naval per every source (RATING) (SCREENER). [F] No percentage split between new-build supply and MRO/spares is disclosed in the documents we have.
Geography split: [F] not disclosed. [MC] The company says it has 'earned the trust of major domestic shipyards as well as international OEMs' (PPT Dec 2025). No export revenue figure is given.

Customer profile: [F] CRISIL says customers are 'government arms and organisations involved in the defence and shipbuilding', and that the company holds Authorised Equipment Manufacturer (AEM) status with DPSU shipyards and Navy Dockyards (RATING). [F] No customer is named and no top-customer revenue share is disclosed.
Scale: [F] FY26 revenue Rs 209 cr, EBITDA Rs 59 cr (28% margin), PAT Rs 39 cr (NUMBERS). [MC] Workforce of '250+ professionals' (PPT Dec 2025).

blocks.text: Evidence base: [F] the company listed on the BSE SME platform and migrated to the BSE Main Board effective 16 September 2026 (RATING) (ANNOUNCEMENTS). [F] As an SME issuer it reported half-yearly, so our statements data has half-year periods, not quarters (NUMBERS). No annual report, prospectus/FPO offer document or earnings-call transcript was available for this report. Segment, customer, related-party, contingent-liability and audit disclosures therefore could not be examined. **Much of what follows is 'not disclosed' in the evidence we have, and that is itself a finding.**

blocks.text: Driver classification: [AI] #2, #3 and #5 are company-specific (qualification, partnerships, installed base). #1 and #4 are partly cyclical, since they depend on naval procurement and tender timing. #7 is a one-off technical event. The only structural driver is the policy push for indigenous naval content, and the documents support it only through the company's own 'Aatmanirbhar' framing [MC] (PPT Dec 2025).

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. Valuation is far above every scenario in our model. [F] Price Rs 1,104 vs DCF per-share values of Rs 109.9 (bear), Rs 186.0 (base) and Rs 262.5 (bull) (NUMBERS). [E] The reverse DCF implies about 95.6% annual sales growth for five years, against a base-case equivalent of 19.8% (NUMBERS).

2. Profits have not turned into cash. [F] CFO was negative in FY23-FY26 (-9, -27, -3, -26 Rs cr) while PAT rose from 10 to 39 (NUMBERS). [E] Cumulative 3-year CFO/PAT is -0.70x and 5-year FCF is -Rs 101 cr (NUMBERS).
3. Receivables are stretching. [F] Debtor days were 183 in FY26 vs 30 in FY24 (NUMBERS). [F] CRISIL puts receivables at 189 days and gross current assets at 400 days (RATING).

4. Growth has been equity-funded. [F] Equity capital rose from Rs 14 cr (FY23) to Rs 21 cr (FY26) (NUMBERS). [F] An FPO in July 2025 raised Rs 94.29 cr net in H1 FY26 (PPT Dec 2025) (RATING). [AI] Two raises in about three years, while CFO stayed negative, is the pattern of a business whose working-capital intensity consumes its growth.

5. Concentration on one end buyer. [F] All revenue relates to Indian naval programmes (RATING) (SCREENER). [F] CRISIL flags revenue and profitability as volatile because the business depends on tenders (RATING). [F] Customer concentration is not disclosed.

6. Opaque current assets. [F] Short-term loans and advances rose from Rs 25.0 cr (Mar 2025) to Rs 62.4 cr (Sep 2025), a Rs 44.6 cr cash outflow in H1 FY26 under 'short-term loans and advances and other current assets' (PPT Dec 2025). The nature of these balances is not disclosed; CRISIL mentions retention money and advances to suppliers (RATING).

7. Internal inconsistency in the H1 FY26 cash-flow statement. [F] Closing cash per the cash-flow statement is Rs 19.42 cr vs Rs 6.33 cr on the balance sheet (PPT Dec 2025). [E] That is a Rs 13.1 cr gap, left unexplained.

8. Modest scale and two sites in one state. [F] CRISIL flags modest scale that constrains pricing and bargaining power (RATING). [F] Both factories are in Maharashtra, with ~7,950 sq m combined covered area (RATING).

9. Thin disclosure. [F] No segment, customer, geography, capacity or order-execution schedule is disclosed in the available documents. [AI] That makes the order book unverifiable at contract level beyond two announced orders totalling Rs 43.14 cr [E] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

Is the order book worth the multiple? [AI] A 2.6x book-to-revenue ratio [E] supports roughly 25-35% growth for 1-2 years, but it does not support the ~96% five-year CAGR the price implies [E] (NUMBERS). A market that extrapolates the order book into a much larger opportunity may be wrong on the upside. A market that ignores the order book may be wrong the other way.

Is the working capital structural or year-end timing? [F] CRISIL attributes high receivables to 'higher year-end sales' and expects the working-capital requirement to 'remain large over the medium term' (RATING). [AI] If receivables normalise from 183 days to the FY23-FY24 level (30-42 days), cash conversion would change sharply. Nothing in the documents shows this happening.

Is the promoter stake falling because of selling or dilution? [E] The 5.24-point drop (73.30% to 68.06%) matches exactly the arithmetic dilution from 15 lakh new FPO shares (73.30% x 1,947.41/2,097.41 = 68.06%) (NUMBERS) (PPT Dec 2025). [AI] The 'promoters selling' flag in the rule-based screen, and in earlier board notes, is therefore probably wrong: this is FPO dilution, not a sale.

Are margins sustainable? [F] EBITDA margin has held at 26-29% for five years (NUMBERS). [AI] That consistency across a tender-based, lumpy business argues for pricing discipline or a niche position. Without product mix data, we cannot tell whether it survives larger, more competitive tenders.
Does Main Board migration change anything fundamental? [AI] It changes liquidity, index eligibility and probably reporting frequency. It does not change cash conversion.

blocks.text: [AI] The consensus narrative, reflected in our own earlier board notes, frames CFF as a scarce indigenisation play with a deep moat, and treats the falling promoter stake as a warning sign. We think both halves are mis-weighted. The promoter 'selling' is FPO dilution [E] (NUMBERS). The more important unpriced issue is cash. Over FY22-FY26 CFF reported Rs 98 cr of cumulative PAT but Rs -50 cr of cumulative CFO [E] (NUMBERS), and it funded the gap with an IPO and an FPO. At Rs 1,104 the market is paying about 59x trailing earnings (NUMBERS) for earnings that have not yet shown they convert to cash. The bull case needs a demonstrable collapse in receivable days, not just more orders.

subsections.title: Where value is captured and capital intensity

blocks.text: [AI] Value is captured in qualification and systems integration, not in machining. That explains a gross margin proxy of roughly 40-43% [E] (PPT Dec 2025) and EBITDA margins near 28% (NUMBERS) on a small fixed-asset base. [F] Fixed assets were Rs 31 cr against FY26 revenue of Rs 209 cr, a fixed-asset turnover of 6.74x (NUMBERS).

[F] The real capital intensity is in working capital. Other assets, mostly current assets, were Rs 276 cr of Rs 317 cr total assets in FY26, i.e. 87% [E] (NUMBERS). [AI] This is an asset-light but working-capital-heavy model. Each rupee of growth ties up inventory, receivables, retention money and supplier advances well before cash is received.

blocks.text: [F] The company does not disclose revenue, volumes or margins by product line (NUMBERS) (PPT Dec 2025). Every competitive and margin judgment above is our inference.

[AI] The differentiated lines are those that need partner technology and submarine qualification: sonar, weapon handling, buoyant wire antennas and HP-air fluid systems. Steering gear, HVAC and test rigs look closer to build-to-print engineering, where L1 (lowest-bidder) tendering compresses margins. [F] CRISIL notes 'different products providing varied profitability' (RATING). The mix is not disclosed, so we cannot tell which lines drive the 28% EBITDA margin.
[F] Segment margins are not disclosed. [AI] The company appears to report as a single segment, which is typical for an SME issuer, but we could not confirm this without the annual report.

items: [MC] Management attributes the trajectory to 'continuous innovation and development' and partnerships with global defence leaders (PPT Dec 2025). It gives no volume, price or programme bridge.
[F] CRISIL attributes growth to tie-ups 'along with the strong execution capabilities' (RATING).

[AI] Our read: growth is order-driven. The whole business is tender-based (RATING), and H2 FY25 revenue (Rs 66 cr) was lower than H1 FY25 (Rs 80 cr) before H1 FY26 jumped to Rs 104 cr (NUMBERS). That is lumpy execution, not organic run-rate growth.

sections.title: Export vs domestic and geographic exposure

blocks.text: [AI] The customer description (Indian Navy, DPSU shipyards, Navy Dockyards) suggests revenue is almost entirely domestic (RATING). [MC] The claim of 'international OEMs' as customers (PPT Dec 2025) is not quantified. [F] The 3 Sep 2026 order is described as 'domestic' (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

subsections.title: Currency, trade policy and location risk

items: [F] H1 FY26 shows a foreign exchange fluctuation loss of Rs 0.45 cr vs a gain of Rs 0.08 cr in H1 FY25 (PPT Dec 2025). [AI] This points to foreign-currency payables or receivables, probably imported components or licence payments to European partners. Hedging policy is not disclosed.
[F] No tariff or trade-policy exposure is discussed in any document. [AI] The relevant risk is export-licence or technology-transfer approvals from France and Germany, not tariffs; none is disclosed.
[F] Both plants are in Maharashtra: Khopoli (Raigad) and Chakan (Pune) (RATING). [AI] Mechanical and electronics lines sit in different plants, so one site outage would stop a whole product family.

blocks.text: Two ways to read it: [F] CRISIL calls the customer base 'diversified', covering 'government arms and organisations involved in the defence and shipbuilding' (RATING). [AI] At the contracting level this may be true, since there are several shipyards and dockyards. At the end-user level, every rupee ultimately depends on Indian Navy budgets and programme timing. The contracting-level view looks diversified; the budget-level view is maximally concentrated.

[F] No long-term agreement is disclosed. The two announced orders are fixed-scope supply contracts with delivery dates (ANNOUNCEMENTS). [AI] Revenue appears to be purchase-order/tender based.

blocks.text: [AI] Overall read: CFF's relationships are gated by qualification. That usually makes them sticky once won, but it also caps the number of clients. Without named contracts or revenue by client, wallet-share upside cannot be assessed. The evidence supports 'approved supplier to the Indian naval ecosystem' and nothing more granular.

[MC] Management's H1 FY26 presentation states 'Order Book Rs. 54,000 Lakhs+ as on 14th November 2025' (PPT Dec 2025). [F] CRISIL reports a 'healthy order book of ~Rs 551 crore as of July 3, 2026' (RATING). CRISIL does not independently audit company information (RATING). [F] No L1 positions, tender pipeline or execution schedule are disclosed.

[AI] The order book rose only ~Rs 11 cr between Nov 2025 and Jul 2026 [E], while the company booked Rs 105 cr of revenue in H2 FY26 alone (NUMBERS) plus unknown Q1 FY27 revenue. Inflows therefore at least matched execution, but the book is not compounding as fast as revenue. [E] Its ratio to revenue fell from ~3.7x FY25 to ~2.6x FY26.

[F] Its latest announced order is a Rs 27.85 cr submarine equipment contract (ANNOUNCEMENTS). [AI] It sits at tier 1/tier 2 below the shipyard prime, supplying subsystems. Narrative only: [MC] the board-note claim that CFF displaces imported systems 'from Russia, France and other OEM-source countries' comes from our earlier internal notes, not from company disclosure (BOARD). The company documents do not quantify import substitution.

[F] Atlas Elektronik (Germany) is named as a partner (PPT Dec 2025). [AI] This is the newest line and the most important one for the differentiation argument, but its revenue is not disclosed.

blocks.text: [F] No installed capacity, output or utilisation figure is disclosed, so no utilisation trend can be built. [AI] A capacity-based revenue sensitivity would be fabricated, so we do not present one. The proxy we can build is fixed-asset turnover: 2.73x in FY23, 3.57x in FY24, 4.06x in FY25 and 6.74x in FY26 (NUMBERS). [AI] Revenue grew much faster than the asset base, so the existing plants were being sweated harder. [F] CWIP of Rs 11 cr at FY26 (NUMBERS) suggests the next increment is under way.

[E] Sensitivity, not base case: if the FY26 fixed-asset turnover of 6.74x (NUMBERS) held on gross block including the FY26 CWIP of Rs 11 cr, the asset base could support revenue in the region of the current order book run-rate. We do not quantify this further because capacity is not disclosed. Lease expiries are not disclosed.
[F] Capex, capex/sales and CWIP from our statements data (NUMBERS); capex/EBITDA is our calculation. [F] H1 FY26 purchase of PPE was Rs 2.73 cr (PPT Dec 2025), so most FY26 capex fell in H2 [E].

items: [E] FY23 to FY26: revenue +Rs 138 cr (71 to 209) against cumulative capex of Rs 31 cr (FY24-FY26), about 4.5x incremental sales per rupee of capex (NUMBERS).
[E] Over the same period total assets rose Rs 228 cr (89 to 317), so incremental sales per rupee of total capital employed were only ~0.6x (NUMBERS). The capital went into working capital, not plant.

[F] Planned capex, project scope and funding are not disclosed. [F] CRISIL lists 'large, debt-funded capital expenditure' as a downgrade trigger (RATING), which implies no such plan is currently assumed.

blocks.text: [AI] Classification: asset-light in fixed capital, capital-heavy in working capital.

[F] Cost of materials consumed was Rs 54.7 cr in H1 FY26, Rs 24.0 cr in H2 FY25 and Rs 20.7 cr in H1 FY25, before changes in inventories (PPT Dec 2025). [F] The specific inputs (metals, electronic components, licensed assemblies), import share by year and by country, and supplier names are not disclosed. [F] CRISIL cites long lead times for critical components as the reason for high inventory (RATING). [F] The Rs 0.45 cr H1 FY26 FX loss (PPT Dec 2025) points to some import or foreign-currency content [AI].

[F] No commodity price trend data is in the documents. [F] Pass-through ability is not discussed by management. [AI] Fixed-price defence tenders with 12-18 month delivery windows (ANNOUNCEMENTS) usually limit pass-through within a contract. The stable 26-29% EBITDA margin (NUMBERS) suggests input risk has been bid in so far.

items: FY22: [AI] margin step-up from 19% to 27% on revenue tripling (NUMBERS). Operating leverage on a very small base, likely cyclical.
FY24: [AI] 29% peak as revenue passed Rs 100 cr (NUMBERS).

FY25-FY26: [F] flat at 28% (NUMBERS). [AI] No further operating leverage despite 43% growth. Employee and other expenses rose as a share of revenue in H1 FY26 (PPT Dec 2025) [E], consistent with building capability at Chakan.

[AI] Materials and 'operative expenses' swap between each other half to half (operative 26.8% in H2 FY25 vs 6.3% in H1 FY26). This suggests job mix (subcontracted work vs material-heavy supply) drives the cost lines, while the combined gross margin proxy stays at 40-43% [E].

blocks.text: [AI] Bottom line: the margin is stable, not improving. Five years at 26-29% across a lumpy order book is a real signal of pricing discipline. PAT margin expansion from 16% to 19% (FY25 to FY26) came from lower interest, flat depreciation and a lower tax rate of 25% vs 28% (NUMBERS), not from operations.

subsections.title: What can and cannot be built

blocks.text: [F] Volumes, units shipped, system counts, capacity and per-contract pricing are not disclosed. A blended realisation / material cost / contribution per unit table cannot be built without inventing numbers, so we do not present one. [E] What can be said: per rupee of revenue in H1 FY26, about 57 paise went to materials and operative expenses, 7.5 paise to employees, 7.3 paise to other expenses, and about 28 paise was left as EBITDA (PPT Dec 2025). [E] The Rs 27.85 cr and Rs 15.29 cr contracts (ANNOUNCEMENTS) are the only disclosed contract-level values.

subsections.title: What would need to be true for unit economics to improve

[F] Our DCF model runs a 5-year FCFF (EBITDA less tax on EBIT, capex and change in net working capital), fades growth linearly to a year-5 rate, and applies a Gordon terminal value (NUMBERS). [F] Base inputs: TTM sales Rs 209 cr, EBITDA margin 28%, starting growth 30% (median of 3-year, 5-year and TTM growth, capped at 30%), D&A 2.9% of sales, working-capital days 285.7, tax 25.2%, WACC 15.0% (cost of equity 15.0%, beta 1.15), terminal growth 5.5%, 2.097 cr shares (NUMBERS).

[AI] Drivers: FCFF stays negative for two years because the model carries ~286 working-capital days on incremental sales. That mirrors FY23-FY26 history (NUMBERS). [AI] Year-1 growth of 30% is covered by the ~Rs 551 cr order book (RATING) if execution continues at the FY26 pace.

items: Revenue = order book at start of year x execution rate + new orders executed within the year (none of these components is disclosed).
EBITDA = revenue x (1 - materials/operative share ~57% - employee ~7.5% - other ~7.3%) [E] (PPT Dec 2025).
FCFF = EBITDA - tax - capex (small) - working-capital build (large: the swing factor).
Working capital = receivable days (year-end billing) + inventory days (lead times) + advances/retention (contract terms).

The second contestable assumption is terminal growth of 5.5% after a 5-year fade, which truncates any long-duration indigenisation runway.

[F] The reverse DCF shows today's EV requires about 95.6% constant annual sales growth for five years at a 28% margin, 15% WACC and 5.5% terminal growth. [E] The price implies roughly double the bull case's starting growth, sustained for five years, on a business whose order book covers about 2.6 years of current revenue (RATING) (NUMBERS). **The market is capitalising a growth path that no disclosed order, capacity or guidance supports.**

summary.one_line: CFF Fluid Control is a qualified, profitable, low-debt naval subsystem supplier with a ~Rs 551 cr order book, but its reported profits have not converted to cash and the Rs 1,104 share price sits far above even the bull-case DCF value of Rs 262.5, implying ~96% annual growth that no disclosed evidence supports.
